extracted.intended_audience: fiction authors / writers seeking guidance on writing characters from cultures other than their own
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for fiction writers on how to include characters from cultures other than their own without resorting to cultural appropriation, tokenism, or stereotypes. Covers definitions, contextual judgement, research practices, and character-development techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict definition of cultural appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural appropriation is the adoption of elements from a minority culture by the dominant culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strict definition would label white authors with characters of color, straight authors with LGBTQ characters, and Christian authors with characters from other religions as appropriating. Use this definition to recognize the basic dynamic of dominant-group adoption of minority cultural elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced (Amandla Stenberg) definition of cultural appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural appropriation occurs when a style leads to racist generalizations or stereotypes where it originated, but is deemed as high fashion cool or funny when the privileged take it from themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By this definition, appropriation is context-dependent: the same element can be harmful when borrowed by privileged groups if it perpetuates racist generalizations. Evaluate whether your use causes or reinforces stereotypes or double standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context matters when judging appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation comes down to context and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the context in which cultural elements are used — who is portraying them, to what end, and whether the portrayal fosters racist generalizations. Well-researched, contextualized portrayals are less likely to be appropriative; shallow or sensationalized uses are more likely to be harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing characters to stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Your characters should not be able to be reduced to simply an 'angry black woman,' a 'welfare queen,' a 'thug,' a 'diminutive Asian woman,' an 'exotic beauty,' an 'Asian genius,' a 'fiery Latina,' a 'Mexican drug dealer,' or a 'sassy gay guy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are stereotypes and can be harmful and lazy writing. If a character appears briefly or exists only to move the protagonist along, avoid assigning them stereotypical traits. Anti-pattern: using cultural shorthand as a shorthand for character identity without depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deepen and humanize characters (subvert stereotypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subvert stereotypes by deepening the character beyond the stereotype — give them passions, relationships, contradictions, and a life outside the stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: make the drug dealer also a loving father, a Rhodes scholar, or actually a cop undercover; give a Black woman things that make her happy and a life outside her anger. The goal is to make the character a 'whole person.' Scoring note: richer interior life, multiple roles and motivations, and unexpected traits indicate stronger, non-stereotypical characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tokenism; include fully developed minority characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless some of your fully developed characters are minorities, you're not doing the whole diversity thing right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Token, one-off minor characters are insufficient diversity and may reinforce stereotypes. Where possible, include central, fully developed minority characters rather than only brief or surface-level representations. If a minority character is only in one scene, it's best to avoid stereotyping them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research and lived-experience consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is one of the best ways to make your characters whole — approach character-building like an actor: do tons of research, read source material, find people like your character and learn from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: interview people with the life experience you're writing about; ask about what it was really like, what they miss, how their worldview changed, their social circles. Use context clues from source material. Anti-patterns: relying solely on stereotypes, secondhand hearsay, or cursory online searches. Note that the character will not be the person you interviewed, but the research informs authenticity of mindset, speech patterns, and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow group-associated traits but avoid essentializing
rubrics_metrics.description: It's acceptable for a character to have traits commonly associated with their group (for example, a Black woman getting angry or a Mexican character being a drug dealer), but that cannot be all they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure these traits are one aspect of a multifaceted character rather than the defining or only attribute. Provide motivations, backstory, and other dimensions so the trait doesn't function as an essentialized shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize representation's positive impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation matters — many people in minority groups recall impactful moments when they first saw themselves represented in media (e.g., #FirstTimeISawMe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to weigh the importance of inclusive, respectful portrayal: creating authentic representation can have meaningful positive effects. Avoid practices that might 'represent' a group but only replicate harmful tropes.
